blocks.content: The base image is whatever you name in your Dockerfile's FROM instruction, the starting point every other layer in your image gets built on top of.

The very first (non-comment) line of almost every Dockerfile is a FROM instruction, naming the image everything else builds on. It could be a full Linux distribution, a language runtime that already includes an OS, or something far more minimal.

blocks.alt: FROM picks the foundation everything else builds on

blocks.content:
FROM ubuntu:22.04
FROM node:18
FROM python:3.11-slim
FROM scratch

blocks.content: 2. Base Images Vary Enormously in Size
blocks.text: 2. Base Images Vary Enormously in Size

blocks.content: A full ubuntu base weighs in around 78MB before you have added a single line of your own application. An alpine-based equivalent (built on the minimal Alpine Linux distribution) can be under 10MB. scratch is the extreme case: a completely empty image with nothing in it at all.

blocks.alt: The base you choose sets your image's size floor

blocks.content: 3. Your Layers Stack on the Base's Layers
blocks.text: 3. Your Layers Stack on the Base's Layers

blocks.content: Every layer your own Dockerfile instructions add stacks directly on top of whatever layers the base image itself already contains. Choosing a heavier base does not just cost you disk space once, it is baked into every single image you ever build from it.

blocks.alt: Your layers sit on top of everything the base already brought

blocks.content: FROM scratch gives you a base image with absolutely nothing in it, no shell, no package manager, no libraries. It only makes sense for statically compiled binaries (common with Go or Rust) that do not depend on any shared libraries from an OS to run.

blocks.alt: scratch works only for fully self-contained binaries

blocks.content: {"headers":["Base Image","Typical Size","Best For"],"rows":[["ubuntu / debian","70 to 120 MB","Apps needing a full general-purpose OS and package manager"],["alpine","about 5 to 10 MB","Most production services, minimal footprint with a working shell"],["distroless","a few MB, no shell","Maximum security surface reduction, harder to debug interactively"],["scratch","0 MB","Statically compiled binaries with zero external dependencies"]]}

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: FROM chooses the base image, and every layer you add afterward stacks directly on top of it, so its size and contents affect every build.
alpine is the common default for a small, still-functional base, scratch is for statically compiled binaries with no OS dependency at all.
